title: The golden mouth
hook: John Chrysostom: if you can't find Christ in the beggar at the door, you won't find him in the chalice

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rome falls, and Augustine's two cities. Your line was two cities, two loves.

Silk in the church. Gold cups for the wine. A preacher stands in a church full of beautiful things, and he points past all of it, to the door, and to the man sitting outside it, asking for bread. The preacher is John, a priest of Antioch who later became bishop of Constantinople. People came to call him Chrysostom, which means golden mouth.

The sermon is one of his homilies on Matthew's Gospel. He's speaking of the bread and the cup, the body of Christ at the altar, with deep reverence. Then he turns. Do you want to honor Christ's body? Then don't ignore him when he's naked. Don't honor him in here with silk, while outside you pass him by, cold and without clothes. What good is it if his table is loaded with gold cups, while he himself is dying of hunger? Feed him first. Then adorn his table too. He isn't against beautiful churches. He's against the order being backwards. Where does he get this? From Jesus, in Matthew. At the end of a story about the last judgment, the King says, in the King James words: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." Chrysostom takes that at its word. The person at the door isn't only a reminder of Christ; by that Gospel, what's done to him is done to Christ. The same Christ the congregation is about to receive at the altar is sitting outside, asking. Churches understand the altar differently. Orthodox and Catholic Christians speak of Christ truly present in the bread and wine; Protestant churches understand communion in a range of ways. All of them can hear Chrysostom's question about the door. The golden mouth didn't keep him safe. His preaching against luxury, the luxury of the powerful included, made him enemies, and he died in exile. His sermons are still read, and the question is still in them: did you see him at the door?

Recall someone you've passed who was asking, on a corner, at a station, outside a shop; maybe you gave, maybe you looked away, and there's no verdict either way. See their face again, as a face, and settle on one concrete thing for next time: a coin, a sandwich, a question about their name. If you pray, pray for that person, even without a name.
Chrysostom, the golden mouth. John, the preacher who said the Christ honored at the altar is also asking at the door.
Your line: christ at the door. The same Christ, at the altar and outside it. That's day seven hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Orthodox and Eastern Catholic churches celebrate the Divine Liturgy that bears John Chrysostom's name, and Christians of different churches honor him as a saint and read his sermons, especially on care for the poor.

chat.says: Was Chrysostom against churches having gold cups and silk?
options: Not exactly. Feed Christ in the hungry first, he said, then adorn his table too.
Yes. He wanted every gold cup sold and all beauty stripped from the churches.
No. He said a beautiful altar matters more than the beggar at the door.
chat.meaning: He wasn't against beautiful churches, only the order being backwards: what's done to the least is done to Christ, so feed him first.

notes: The index hook's wording ('if you can't find Christ in the beggar at the door, you won't find him in the chalice') is a popular paraphrase; the script uses the content of Homily 50 on Matthew (honor Christ's body; silk inside, naked outside; gold cups while he starves; feed him first, then adorn the table). Paraphrased; confirm section numbers.
Nickname Chrysostom = 'golden-mouthed' (Greek). The script says 'people came to call him', without dating it. Confirm.
Biography kept minimal: priest of Antioch, later bishop of Constantinople, made enemies by preaching against luxury, died in exile. Confirm the framing of the cause of his exile.

Eucharist views: 'Orthodox and Catholic Christians speak of Christ truly present in the bread and wine; Protestant churches understand communion in a range of ways.' Note that Lutherans and some Anglicans also affirm real presence; Keeper may prefer different wording.
